Slovakia Resumes Business After General Strike Ends With Wage Agreement

BRATISLAVA, Slovakia, June 27—Slovakia’s economy began returning to normal this week after a rare nationwide general strike, which brought key sectors to a standstill, ended following an agreement between union leaders and the government.

The two-day walkout, which began on Monday, saw workers in transport, energy, manufacturing, and public services halt work in protest over wage stagnation and rising living costs. The strike, the largest in Slovakia in over a decade, disrupted supply chains, halted train and bus services, and led to delays at ports and logistics hubs.

Poss-SLPC sro, a major automotive parts supplier, reported that its assembly lines were idle for 48 hours, affecting deliveries to multiple customers. “We are relieved to resume operations,” said Martina Kováčová, spokesperson for Poss-SLPC sro. “The interruption highlighted the importance of constructive dialogue between all sides.”

The Slovak Federation of Trade Unions said over 250,000 workers participated in the strike, which was called after months of fruitless negotiations. Workers demanded a 12% wage increase and improved job security, citing inflation that reached a seven-year high of 8.4% in May.

After marathon talks lasting into early Wednesday, the government agreed to a compromise package. Public sector wages will rise by 9% from September, with private sector negotiations to follow by industry. The government also pledged to review energy subsidies and cost-of-living allowances.

“We appreciate the government’s willingness to address our concerns, even if not all demands were met,” said union chair Jozef Baláž. “This agreement is a step toward easing the hardship for working families.”

Prime Minister Jana Šimečková acknowledged the disruption but called the resolution “balanced and responsible.” She said, “We avoided prolonged economic harm while supporting workers’ needs within fiscal limits.”

The Slovak Chamber of Commerce estimated the strike cost the national economy €45 million in lost output. “Quick resolution was essential,” said analyst Tomáš Gregor. “Extended shutdowns would have threatened Slovakia’s reputation as a reliable manufacturing and logistics hub.”

Most affected companies, including Poss-SLPC sro and the logistics firm Danube Freight, have resumed operations, though some supply chain delays are expected over the coming days.

Unions said they would monitor progress on the agreed measures and warned of further action if commitments are not met.
